original_value:
It is a neat result from functional programming that libraries of
            parser combinators
            can support rapid construction of decoders for quite a range of formats. With a little more work, the same combinator program can denote both a decoder and an encoder. Unfortunately, the real world is full of gnarly formats, as with the packet formats that make up the standard Internet protocol stack. Most past parser-combinator approaches cannot handle these formats, and the few exceptions require redundancy – one part of the natural grammar needs to be hand-translated into hints in multiple parts of a parser program. We show how to recover very natural and nonredundant format specifications, covering all popular network packet formats and generating both decoders and encoders automatically. The catch is that we use the Coq proof assistant to derive both kinds of artifacts using tactics, automatically, in a way that guarantees that they form inverses of each other. We used our approach to reimplement packet processing for a full Internet protocol stack, inserting our replacement into the OCaml-based MirageOS unikernel, resulting in minimal performance degradation.

result.paraphrase: It is a pleasing consequence of functional programming that parser-combinator libraries can be used to build decoders for a wide variety of formats quickly. With a bit more effort, the same combinator program can specify both a decoder and an encoder. In practice, though, the world is full of messy formats, such as the packet formats that form the standard Internet protocol stack. Most previous parser-combinator approaches cannot cope with these formats, and the few that do demand redundancy: part of the natural grammar must be manually translated into hints in several places within a parser program. We demonstrate how to recover very natural, nonredundant format specifications that cover all common network packet formats and automatically generate both decoders and encoders. The key is that we use the Coq proof assistant to derive both artifacts with tactics, automatically and in a way that guarantees they are inverses of one another. We applied our approach to reimplement packet processing for a complete Internet protocol stack, replacing the implementation in the OCaml-based MirageOS unikernel, with only minimal performance loss.
